Fengshan Food Centre.fact: At the hawker centre locals call “85,” Xing Ji serves its minced pork noodles only in soup.

Kaki Bukit 511 Market.fact: At Block 511, the evening hawker stalls include Zhong Newton, which grills satay and chicken wings.

Masjid Al-Ansar.fact: The 2015 rebuild kept the original minaret and added more prayer space and a lift.

Former Princess Theatre.fact: It opened with twin screens, Princess and Raja, in 1983. The last film was Painted Skin in 2008.

Block 216 Market & Food Centre.fact: By 2024, Lee Teck Lee had spent 42 years making you tiao and other fried dough snacks by hand here.

Former Commonwealth Avenue Wet Market.fact: The last surviving market built by the Singapore Improvement Trust reopened as Margaret Market in 2023.

Princess House.fact: Opened in 1957, Princess House became the Housing & Development Board’s first dedicated headquarters.

Tiong Ghee Temple.fact: The 1973 temple replaced one in Boh Beh Kang village, whose Hokkien name means “river without a tail.”

Mujahidin Mosque.fact: Opened in 1977, it was the second mosque completed under Singapore’s Mosque Building Fund.

Former Venus & Golden City Theatres.fact: The neighbourhood’s first two cinemas opened in 1965. Venus could seat about 1,200 people.

Chomp Chomp Food Centre.fact: The centre opened in 1972. “Chomp Chomp” is an English adaptation of the older Teochew name “Tiong Tiong.”

myVillage.fact: Paramount Theatre once stood here. After its screens went dark in 1983, the cinema became a Fitzpatrick’s supermarket.

Church of St Francis Xavier.fact: Father Philippe Meisonnier carried a cloth bag on his evening fundraising rounds for the church, which opened in 1959.

Kensington Park Condominium.fact: The condominium was completed in 1990 on a 999-year lease that dates back to 1878.

Chartwell Drive Park.fact: A community garden shares this pocket park with a playground and a fitness corner.

Round Market (Block 137).fact: When it opened in 1983, planners expected it to be one of the last wet markets HDB would build.

Sun Plaza Park.fact: Seen from above, the paths meet to form a sun at the centre of the park.

Masjid Darul Ghufran.fact: The mosque’s blue cladding earned it the nickname Menara Biru, Malay for “Blue Minaret.”

World Habitat Award Sculpture.fact: The three-metre sculpture copies the trophy for the 1991 World Habitat Award, which recognised innovative town planning.

Church of the Holy Trinity.fact: The church’s design evokes a fish, an early Christian symbol. Its stained glass came from Milan.

Block 78 Air-Raid Shelter.fact: Built into the pre-war flats, the air-raid shelter could hold about 1,600 people.

Monkey God Temple (Eng Hoon Street).fact: The temple began in 1920 in a thatched hut in a taro garden across the street.

Dancing Girl Sculpture.fact: Lim Nang Seng sculpted this 1.2-metre dancer in an Orchard Road car park, finishing it in two weeks.

Bird Corner (Seng Poh Road).fact: In 1984, jazz flautist Herbie Mann played here to the sound of the songbirds.

Seng Poh Road Market.fact: The original market opened in 1951 to give street hawkers a permanent home. The rebuilt market reopened in 2006.

Dragon Playground (Lorong 6).fact: Khor Ean Ghee’s 1979 dragon still stands in its sand pit.

Lian Shan Shuang Lin Monastery.fact: Founded in 1898, Singapore’s oldest Buddhist monastery takes its name from the “Twin Groves of the Lotus Mountain.”

Chung Hwa Medical Institution.fact: At its 1978 opening, more than 400 patients received treatment and medicine for a token consultation fee.

Kim Keat Palm Market.fact: LiXin makes its Teochew fishballs by hand and serves dry noodles with chilli and crisp cracklings.

Bat-Shaped Block 116.fact: The bat-shaped footprint was an HDB experiment. Its long shared corridors are a feature of early public housing.
